draft.title: Kami
card: Kami are the spirits or sacred powers that Shinto followers honour. The word is often translated as god, but kami are not all-powerful in the way that many other traditions describe God.
Kami can be found in nature, such as mountains, rivers, trees and rocks. They can also be linked to particular places, such as a village or a region.
Kami can also be ancestors, such as the spirits of a family's dead, and people of great achievement, such as a respected leader.
Followers show respect to kami through worship and offerings. Kami are thought to be present in the world, not only in a distant place.
draft.remember: Kami are sacred powers present in nature, places, ancestors and people of great achievement.

a.q: Which description of kami best fits Shinto belief?
opts: Sacred powers found in nature, places and people
One all-powerful creator who rules over the world
Human priests who lead worship at local shrines
Written laws that tell followers how to live
a.why: Kami are spirits or sacred powers that can be found in nature, places, ancestors and people of great achievement. The creator option is tempting because kami is often translated as god, but kami are not described as one all-powerful being.
a.clue: Think of where kami can be found, not who leads worship.

b.q: A village in Japan honours the spirit of a large old cedar tree near its edge. How would Shinto followers understand this tree?
opts: As a place where a kami is present
As a founder who began the Shinto religion
As a priest who passes on the teachings
As a statue made only to be looked at
b.why: Shinto followers see kami in nature, so a large old tree can be honoured as the home of a kami. The tree is not a founder, because Shinto has no single founder, and it is not a priest.
b.clue: Kami can be found in nature.

a.best: Sacred powers found in nature, places and people

b.best: As a place where a kami is present
